threat_assessment:
At a tier-4 table, forget the casual-room fantasy that hug reads as harmless. Professional pods have seen Kwain, Itinerant Meddler before, and they know the genre: symmetric draw plus hand-size punishers is a slug deck wearing a gift bow. Expect your 'I haven't done anything' to be discounted from turn two — experienced tables hit the quiet engine player precisely because combo and punisher decks advance in secret (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection). Your signal profile is loud on paper: 8 Game Changers force the bracket-4 floor, and three of them are read instantly. Rhystic Study on turn 2 is priced in at this tier — it draws groans, not removal. Smothering Tithe is not: at a professional table it is removed on sight or the table pays in lockstep, so deploy it when you can use the treasure the same rotation, not as a turn-2 flex. Consecrated Sphinx is the archenemy switch — it does not resolve quietly at tier 4; land it only when you can defend it or when you are ready to be the threat. The other tell they will read: Mystical Tutor at an end step after your first Approach of the Second Sun has resolved means exactly one thing to anyone who has done the reading, and the whole table's interaction turns to your next upkeep — stack 002 verified that the second cast survives only behind counted, held countermagic, so bank Dovin's Veto or Swan Song for the commit, not the setup.

Your real flip points, in order of how fast the table's math changes: (1) engine + punisher both on board — once Iron Maiden or Ebony Owl Netsuke sits next to a Mine effect, every player who counts realizes stack 003's arithmetic (7 damage on the punished upkeep, and cleanup trimming doesn't save them) and the clock is public; (2) Forced Fruition resolving — the loudest card in the deck, a table-wide event that makes you archenemy immediately unless a punisher is already taxing the refill; (3) Heliod flipped to the Warped Eclipse with cards in your grip — professionals know the back face grants flash and discounts off their draws, so from that point your untapped lands are read as interaction even when they aren't. Use that: the flash grant means 'tapped out' stops being a real state for you, and Displacer Kitten deepens the ambiguity — with Kitten out, every noncreature cast untaps or resets something (a blinked Sol Ring returns untapped; a blinked Mystic Remora returns as a new object), and experienced opponents will assume the worst about what your board can do mid-stack. Let them. But know your own ceiling exactly, because stack 005 is now checker-passed and it REFUTES the scary version: adding Kitten to the verified Hullbreaker engine (stack 004) does not make it mana-positive — the loop stays exactly mana-neutral, and the Kitten-first ordering is a one-time, loop-terminating exit that leaves precisely 3 mana floating ({C}{C} plus one colored). Unbounded casts survive; unbounded mana does not exist. So the table's fear of your Kitten board is worth more than the board itself — never play toward an infinite-mana line that a passed stack says isn't there, and price your storm-count exits (a Stroke of Genius, a Secure the Wastes) at X capped by that 3-mana float plus whatever real mana you hold.

Supreme Verdict discipline is its own signal game. Held: against aggro and midrange boards, WWUU open with Heliod flipped is indistinguishable from countermagic, and that ambiguity is the card's second mode — you want them attacking someone else because they can't price your open mana (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math). Telegraphed: in the control mirror or against a permission deck, say it out loud — 'it can't be countered' is a political instrument that redirects the board-committing player's aggression elsewhere (strategy:multiplayer.politics). The Second Doctor is the same trick in permanent form: professionals do the math on the rider, and blanking three players' attack steps for the price of a card each is a trade good pilots accept and then resent — expect the deterrent to buy you two to three real turns before someone eats the card loss to kill the Doctor. Those bought turns are the whole game now, because the rebuild's honest cost is closing speed: wincon access fell to 42.6% by turn 6, and the core two-piece assembles by turn 6 in only 39.6% of games (mean turn 4.2). You got more consistent at the engine (table-draw piece drawn 72.3% by t6) and slower at ending things. So the discipline is: stay small, stay boring, sequence punishers before big draw engines (a lone Iron Maiden is ignored; a lone Howling Mine is welcomed), and do not durdle past your window — when the two-piece is assembled, Heliod's discount is live, and a free counter is in hand, you own inevitability (strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock) and the correct play is to embrace archenemy: the punisher clock runs during draw-go without you tapping out, and at that point every turn the table spends deciding who the threat is, is a turn your upkeeps are killing them (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window).
matchups:
Sweeper control / the control mirror: someone must be the beatdown in a mirror, and it is not you — your clock (stack 003's upkeep damage) advances while both of you draw-go, so you own the long game and can let them act first (strategy:whos-the-beatdown, strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock). Creature wraths hit almost nothing here (mean 1.5 bodies by turn 6 in goldfish); your exposure is artifact/enchantment mass removal taking the Mine layer and the punisher layer together — assume a professional control pilot holds a Farewell-class sweeper, so deploy in layers and never present both punishers to one board state. New in this build: Supreme Verdict is YOUR uncounterable reset — in the mirror it wraths their Torrential Gearhulk board through open permission at zero counterspell cost, which flips who has to commit first. Loran of the Third Path is your repeatable answer posture, and a Displacer Kitten blink re-triggering her ETB is plain oracle text. On Kitten's ceiling, keep the ledger straight: stack 005 (checker: pass) settled the mana question — the Kitten-augmented Hullbreaker loop is refuted as mana-positive, staying mana-neutral with a one-time 3-mana loop-terminating exit — while the Remora age-counter-reset value line is the piece that remains an unverified candidate.

Stax/tax: taxes attack exactly your velocity math — many cheap spells per turn — so recount the hand under the tax before sequencing (strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial). Against an assembling lock you rarely own the long game; the role flips to beatdown and you race the lock's completion. Heliod's per-opponent-draw discount is a partial rebate no other deck gets — Kwain activations and The Second Doctor's end-step gifts keep growing it even under a Sphere effect — and Kitten-blinking Loran gives repeatable lock-piece removal. Answer the compounding second piece, not the first inconvenience; a lone Thalia is an annoyance, Thalia plus Deafening Silence is a funeral.

Aggro: Propaganda, Ghostly Prison, and The Second Doctor's rider are virtual card advantage tripled at a four-player table — each blanks attack plans from three opponents (strategy:card-advantage.virtual) — and professionals respect the rider math even when casuals wouldn't. Hold Supreme Verdict; commit nothing to the board yourself and let the aggro pilot overextend into the uncounterable reset (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math). The trap has a name: Forced Fruition refuels the aggro player's hand seven cards at a time. Never lead with it into an aggro pod — sequence Iron Maiden or Ebony Owl Netsuke first so the refill arrives taxed (stack 003: hands over seven pay on upkeep, and cleanup trims to exactly seven, so the damage lands before the cards are spent).

Combo and storm: this is your hardest read and your discipline test. The free suite — Fierce Guardianship, Force of Negation, Swan Song, An Offer You Can't Refuse, Dovin's Veto — is held by turn 6 in 62.2% of goldfish games (73.3% ever); spend it only on the card that ends the game if it resolves, per the answer-economy bar (strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy). Deck-specific and non-negotiable at tier 4: the hug layer is a liability here. Kwain taps feed a storm pilot's count, The Second Doctor's gift is a free card to the person assembling a kill, and Forced Fruition against spellslinger is close to suicidal — seven cards per spell to the one player who profits from raw cards. Against a known combo seat, Kwain stays untapped, the Doctor's offer goes to the other two players only, and Fruition stays in hand unless a punisher is already down and you are the one about to win. Your own race line — Mystical Tutor into the second Approach (stack 002) — exists, but with wincon access at 42.6% by t6 you usually are not the faster deck; your winning posture is warden, not racer, until the pivot window opens (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window).

Graveyard decks and incidental hate: mostly a non-event — the deck asks nothing of its graveyard except Dig Through Time's delve and Torrential Gearhulk's flashback target, so opposing Rest in Peace costs you a card's worth of value, not a plan. Conversely you bring no graveyard interaction at all; against a reanimator seat your only answers are the counterspell suite and Path/Swords on the reanimated body — budget the free counters accordingly, because that seat's game-ender bar is met early and often.
how_it_wins:
This deck hands the whole table a firehose of cards, then charges for the water. The engines — Howling Mine, Font of Mythos, Temple Bell, Dictate of Kruphix, Kami of the Crescent Moon, Folio of Fancies, and above all Forced Fruition — are perfectly symmetric on their face, and the new hug layer leans into it: Kwain offers everyone a card (and a life), The Second Doctor offers another at your end step. The punishers make the generosity anything but kind: Iron Maiden and Viseling deal upkeep damage equal to hand size minus 4, and Ebony Owl Netsuke deals a flat 4 to anyone at seven or more cards. Stack 003 verified the arithmetic that makes this a real clock: once Forced Fruition has filled a hand, cleanup trims the opponent to exactly 7 cards, and the next upkeep Owl hits for 4 and Maiden for 3 — 7 damage, from you, without tapping a single land. And that 7 is now the floor, not the ceiling: The Second Doctor's 'Players have no maximum hand size' means the cleanup trim never happens, so a ten-card hand takes 6 from the Maiden instead of 3 while the Owl keeps firing. Both artifacts trigger on each opponent's upkeep, so the tax runs three ways while you sit behind a counter suite the goldfish sim says you're holding in 73% of games — with Supreme Verdict, the uncounterable reset this deck previously lacked, waiting for the board states countermagic can't fix.

The clean kill is Approach of the Second Sun. The first cast gains 7 life — 14 with Alhammarret's Archive out — and buries the card seventh from the top: trivially shallow in a deck where everyone draws in bulk and two doublers (Archive, Teferi's Ageless Insight) accelerate your own digging, or Mystical Tutor and Long-Term Plans put it back on top directly. Stack 002 verified the second cast end to end: the win condition is checked during resolution, as a spell effect, and the first casting still counts because the game tracks the casting event in its history, not the card that got shuffled away. The opponents' only window is while the second Approach is on the stack. One honest cost of the rebuild: with White Sun's Zenith moved to the pool, win-condition access is drawn by turn 6 in only 42.6% of goldfish runs, down from 50% — the tutors carry more of the weight now, so commit on the turn you can protect it, because once resolution begins, nothing stops it.

The third piece is an engine, not a win: Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring + a two-mana rock (stack 004). Each rock's cast triggers the Horror to bounce the other rock — a legal target, because at that moment it is a permanent — and tapping each rock before it bounces makes the cycle exactly mana-neutral: 3 spent, 3 produced, unbounded casts in a single main phase. It nets zero mana, zero cards, zero damage on its own. The flagged lethal outlet is Aetherflux Reservoir — 1 life per spell cast this turn (doubled by the Archive), then Pay 50 life for 50 damage — but that line has not been stack-verified; treat it as a candidate, not a fact. Displacer Kitten's promise of making the loop mana-positive, by contrast, is settled: stack 005 refutes it — the loop stays exactly neutral, with a one-time +1-mana exit. And know what the deck does NOT do: the combo database's two-card Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring 'infinite' is refuted (stack 001). The pair alone produces nothing.

Heliod is the hinge that makes all of it asymmetric. The front face rebuys an enchantment on arrival; a sorcery-speed {3}{U/P} flips him into the Warped Eclipse, which grants everything flash and discounts your spells by {1} for each card your opponents drew this turn — and every card an opponent accepts from Kwain or the Second Doctor grows that discount on the turn you want to act. The goldfish sim has Heliod down by turn 6 in 90.8% of games (mean turn 4.1), the deck's most reliable single event, and the rebuild's engine additions lifted the core two-piece — table engine plus punisher — to 39.6% assembled by turn 6, up from 34.3%. Still not automatic: most games you play draw-go control while the pieces gather, and the deck is built to be good at exactly that.

combo_lines.001: What this deck does NOT do. The combo database lists Hullbreaker Horror + Sol Ring as a two-card infinite (296,000 decks believe it); this walk refutes it. The Horror's trigger is modal, and mode and target lock in while the Sol Ring that caused it is still a spell on the stack — a spell you control is not a legal target for 'target spell you don't control,' and it is not a nonland permanent either. By the time Sol Ring is a permanent, the trigger is gone. The pair alone loops nothing: no mana, no storm count. Never pitch this deck to the table — or compute its bracket — on the strength of that database line.
combo_lines.002: The second Approach of the Second Sun, put on top by Mystical Tutor and cast from your hand. The two questions that decide games: yes, the first casting still counts even though the card was shuffled back into your library — the condition checks an event in the game's history, not the card object — and the win is checked mid-resolution, as a spell effect, not a state-based action. The opponents' one and only window is while Approach sits on the stack; the walk plays out the counter-war, including Swan Song answering their counterspell with {U} held. Once all players pass and resolution begins, the game simply ends.
combo_lines.003: The punisher core doing its job under fire. An opponent tries to Naturalize Forced Fruition — and the Fruition trigger sits on top of the very spell that caused it, so they draw their seven cards before the enchantment dies (and the ability would survive its source's destruction anyway). Cleanup trims them to exactly 7 in hand, which is precisely the threshold both punishers want: next upkeep, Ebony Owl Netsuke's intervening-if sees seven cards and deals 4, Iron Maiden deals 7 minus 4 = 3, for 7 total. Both triggers are yours, so you order them — though here neither changes hand size, so the math is order-proof.
combo_lines.004: The real Hullbreaker engine — three cards, not two. Cast the two-mana rock; the Horror's trigger targets Sol Ring, which IS a legal target because it's on the battlefield, a permanent, not a spell. Tap Sol Ring for {C}{C} while the trigger is on the stack (a mana ability — nothing can respond), let the bounce resolve, recast Sol Ring, bounce and tap the Signet in turn. One full cycle: 3 mana spent, 3 produced — exactly mana-neutral, so the cast count is unbounded within one main phase off a {2} investment. It nets no mana, cards, or damage by itself, and aiming a trigger at an opponent's permanent breaks the chain. Thought Vessel substitutes for Arcane Signet exactly; Fellwar Stone only while an opponent's land can actually produce mana.
combo_lines.005: What the Kitten does NOT do to the engine. The hope: Displacer Kitten blinks Sol Ring untapped mid-loop, and stack 004's mana-neutral cycle goes mana-positive. This walk refutes it. Both of your triggers lock their targets at announcement, and whichever resolves first turns the shared useful target into a new object — so the second trigger's target is illegal and it fizzles. Horror's bounce and the Kitten's blink are mutually exclusive on every cast. Keep the loop alive and the Kitten contributes exactly nothing: the cycle stays exactly 3 spent, 3 produced. Blink first and you really do tap Sol Ring twice on that cast — but Horror's bounce fizzles, your hand empties, and the loop TERMINATES: a one-time exit worth 3 floating mana against the best Kitten-less exit's 2. Unbounded casts survive untouched; unbounded mana does not exist, and an X spell off this engine is capped at that terminal float of at most 3.

card_roles.Heliod, the Radiant Dawn // Heliod, the: Front face: a 4/4 that returns a non-God enchantment from your graveyard on arrival — Forced Fruition or Rhystic Study back after a wrath is the usual pick. The {3}{U/P} flip (sorcery speed, payable with 2 life) turns on the deck: the Warped Eclipse grants all your spells flash and discounts them {1} per card your opponents drew this turn — your own table-draw engines, Kwain activations, and Second Doctor end-step gifts pay your costs while you keep mana up for counters.
card_roles.Forced Fruition: The punisher core's detonator: every opponent spell is seven forced draws, feeding Iron Maiden, Ebony Owl Netsuke, and Viseling past their thresholds instantly. Stack 003 verified the trigger resolves even when the spell it triggered on is the removal that kills it.
card_roles.Iron Maiden: Hand-size-minus-4 damage at each opponent's upkeep, computed on resolution. Inert against a five-card hand; a three-a-turn clock once the engines are running — and with The Second Doctor removing the cleanup trim, the count climbs past stack 003's floor of 3.
card_roles.Ebony Owl Netsuke: A flat 4 at each opponent's upkeep at seven-plus cards — the intervening-if is checked both at trigger and on resolution. With Iron Maiden, exactly 7 damage per punished upkeep off a cleanup-trimmed hand (stack 003); with The Second Doctor keeping hands untrimmed, the check just keeps passing.
card_roles.Viseling: Iron Maiden with a body — same hand-minus-4 upkeep damage on a 1/1 construct. Redundancy for the deck's core clock; dies to creature removal (and your own Supreme Verdict) where the Maiden doesn't.
card_roles.Kwain, Itinerant Meddler: The political engine, new in this build: {T} lets each player draw, and drawers gain 1 life. Every card an opponent accepts inches them toward the punisher thresholds and grows Heliod's discount; every card they decline is a card behind. Your side of the tap doubles twice under Alhammarret's Archive — two cards and 2 life — and a two-mana body that makes the whole table like you buys exactly the waiting turns a 39.6%-by-turn-6 two-piece needs.
card_roles.The Second Doctor: 'Players have no maximum hand size' is the quiet punisher enabler: opponents never trim at cleanup, so Ebony Owl's 7+ check keeps passing and Iron Maiden's hand-minus-4 grows unbounded — while you hoard your own doubled draws without needing Reliquary Tower. The end-step rider is a pillow fort on legs: each opponent who accepts the draw can't attack you or your permanents next turn, stacking with Propaganda and Ghostly Prison, and the cards they take feed the Maiden anyway. Heads they can't attack, tails they fall behind.
card_roles.Alhammarret's Archive: The asymmetry hinge for both of the deck's currencies: every draw of yours after the first in your draw step becomes two, and all your lifegain doubles. Kwain's tap pays you double on both halves, the Mine effects become personal Fonts on your side only, a first Approach of the Second Sun banks 14 life instead of 7, and it stacks with Teferi's Ageless Insight as a second your-side draw doubler. Five mana that converts every symmetric engine you run into a rigged one.
card_roles.Supreme Verdict: The uncounterable reset this deck lacked: four mana, destroy all creatures, and the blue player can do nothing about it. Your clock lives in artifacts and enchantments, so the wrath is nearly one-sided — it does take Kwain, Kami, and your other engine bodies, so time it for when the board, not your own value layer, is the problem.
card_roles.Psychosis Crawler: Drains each opponent for 1 per card YOU draw, and its stats track your hand. With the X-draw suite and the doublers it converts a big refill into table-wide reach — a candidate line flagged for stack verification, not yet walked.
card_roles.Scrawling Crawler: A symmetric upkeep draw stapled to an asymmetric tax: each opponent draw costs them a life, so every engine on your board turns it into a slow burn.
card_roles.Sphinx's Tutelage: Turns your own draws into repeated two-card mills with a shared-color cascade — an alternate attrition angle that scales with the draw doublers and the wheels.
card_roles.Howling Mine: The classic symmetric engine: an extra draw at each draw step while untapped. Symmetric on its face; the punishers, the Archive, and Heliod's discount make it yours.
card_roles.Font of Mythos: Howling Mine doubled — two extra draws for everyone. The fastest way to push the table to seven cards, and the biggest per-turn Heliod discount.
card_roles.Temple Bell: A draw for everyone on demand, at instant speed — which means you can ring it on an opponent's upkeep after their draw step to push a hand over the punisher threshold, or in response to removal for pure value.
card_roles.Dictate of Kruphix: The flash Howling Mine — deploy it end of turn, ahead of the opponent whose upkeep you most want taxed.
card_roles.Kami of the Crescent Moon: Howling Mine on legs for two mana. Cheapest engine in the deck; also the most fragile.
card_roles.Folio of Fancies: Three jobs: removes YOUR maximum hand size, force-feeds the table X cards at once, and can mill an opponent for their whole (bloated) hand. The X-draw activation is the precision tool for pushing hands over 7 at the right moment.
card_roles.Horn of Greed: Draws on every land play — modest for opponents (one land a turn), steady for you, and another trigger keeping hands fat.
card_roles.Rhystic Study: The asymmetric half of the value layer: every opponent spell is a card or a tax, and in a deck this dense with forced action it is a firehose. The Warped Eclipse doesn't discount off it (it counts draws, and Study's draws are yours) — but it wins the card war that decides control mirrors.
card_roles.Mystic Remora: Rhystic Study's early-game twin — a turn-1 Remora often draws three-plus cards before the cumulative upkeep bites. Pay a couple of ages, then let it go — or don't: a Displacer Kitten blink returns it as a new object with no age counters, and the tax restarts from zero.
card_roles.Smothering Tithe: Every opponent draw is {2} or a Treasure for you — and this deck makes opponents draw in sevens. Forced Fruition plus Tithe presents seven pay-or-treasure decisions per opponent spell (flagged for stack verification of the exact yield).
card_roles.Consecrated Sphinx: Two cards to you for every card an opponent draws. Under any table engine this is obscene; under Forced Fruition it is fourteen cards per opponent spell. The single strongest magnet for removal you play.
card_roles.Teferi's Ageless Insight: Doubles every draw of yours past the first each draw step — your Howling Mines become personal Fonts, and digging seven cards to a buried Approach takes half the turns. Stacks with Alhammarret's Archive.
card_roles.Faerie Mastermind: Flash body that pays you a card whenever an opponent draws their second card each turn — free value under your own engines — with an activated Temple Bell stapled on for pushing hands at instant speed.
card_roles.Hullbreaker Horror: An uncounterable flash 7/8 that bounces a spell or permanent on every cast you make — tempo monster in the mid game, and the heart of the verified three-card cast engine with Sol Ring plus any true two-mana rock (stack 004). The two-card 'infinite' with Sol Ring alone is refuted (stack 001).
card_roles.Displacer Kitten: Blinks one of your nonland permanents on each noncreature cast — and in a 99 that is mostly noncreature spells, that is constantly. The oracle-grounded payoffs: a blinked Mystic Remora returns as a new object with zero age counters, so the cumulative upkeep resets (the long-run value of that free Remora is still a candidate line, not yet walked); a blinked tapped Sol Ring returns untapped; a blinked Loran or Faerie Mastermind re-triggers and untaps for another activation. One question is now settled, and the answer is no: stack 005 refutes the hope that the Kitten makes the stack-004 loop mana-positive — target lock at announcement plus the new-object rule make its blink and Horror's bounce mutually exclusive on every cast, so the loop stays exactly mana-neutral, and blinking Sol Ring is a one-time, loop-terminating exit worth +1 floating mana.
card_roles.Sol Ring: The best rock in the format and one of the two battlefield pieces of the verified Hullbreaker loop — the loop taps it for {C}{C} with the bounce trigger already on the stack.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Fixes into either color and serves as the third piece of the 004 engine: its cast bounces Sol Ring, its tap keeps the cycle at exactly 3-in, 3-out.
card_roles.Thought Vessel: Two jobs verified or textual: an exact substitute for Arcane Signet in the Hullbreaker loop (same neutral ledger, per stack 004), and no-maximum-hand-size insurance that survives the creature wraths The Second Doctor doesn't.
card_roles.Fellwar Stone: Ramp that reads opponents' lands — and a conditional loop piece: it sustains the 004 engine only while an opponent controls a land that produces mana; on an empty board the cycle goes mana-negative and the loop dies.
card_roles.Fierce Guardianship: Free countermagic while Heliod is out — the card that lets you tap out for an engine piece and still say no. Part of why the sim shows interaction held in 73% of games.
card_roles.Force of Negation: The other free counter: pitch a blue card on an opponent's turn to stop a noncreature spell and exile it. Guards the punisher board through your tapped-out turns.
card_roles.Swan Song: One mana, counters the counterspell aimed at your second Approach — the exact play walked in stack 002. The 2/2 Bird is a bargain against winning the game.
card_roles.An Offer You Can't Refuse: One-mana noncreature counter; the two Treasures you hand over are a real cost, so aim it at spells that matter — sweepers, counters in the Approach war.
card_roles.Dovin's Veto: The argument-ender: can't be countered itself. The premium hold for your commit turn.
card_roles.Counterspell: The unconditional classic. Two blue is easy in a 36-source blue base.
card_roles.Arcane Denial: Counters anything for {1}{U} and replaces itself next upkeep; the two cards it feeds the opponent are, in this deck, more fuel for your punishers.
card_roles.Approach of the Second Sun: The clean wincon. First cast: 7 life — 14 under Alhammarret's Archive — and seventh from the top, shallow when everyone's drawing in bulk. Second cast from hand wins during resolution, verified end to end in stack 002; the only window to stop it is on the stack. With White Sun's Zenith in the pool, this line carries more of the wincon weight: 42.6% access by turn 6, so lean on the tutors.
card_roles.Aetherflux Reservoir: Life per spell per cast, then Pay 50 life: 50 damage. The natural payoff for the 004 cast engine, Archive-doubled lifegain, and Heliod-discounted flurries — but the lethal line is a flagged candidate awaiting a stack scenario, not a verified fact.
card_roles.Secure the Wastes: Instant-speed X warriors: a board out of nowhere with all your held-up mana at someone's end step, or emergency blockers.
card_roles.Monastery Mentor: Every noncreature spell — most of the deck — makes a prowess monk. Under a Heliod discount turn it converts a cheap flurry into a real board.
card_roles.Metallurgic Summonings: Constructs sized to each instant or sorcery you cast; the buyback clause returns your whole spell graveyard once you control six artifacts, which this deck reaches without trying.
card_roles.Mystical Tutor: The Approach enabler: end-step tutor puts the second copy on top for the win next turn (stack 002's setup). Also finds Supreme Verdict or the right counterspell on demand — and with wincon access at 42.6% by turn 6, it is doing more work than ever.
card_roles.Long-Term Plans: Any card, third from the top — with your draw density and two doublers that's one turn away. Unlike Mystical Tutor it can fetch permanents: Aetherflux, a punisher, the missing loop rock.
card_roles.Mathemagics: Draws 2^X cards — the most explosive refill in the deck and the scariest thing to point at yourself with Psychosis Crawler out (candidate line, unverified).
card_roles.Prosperity: Symmetric X-draw for the table: pushes every hand toward punisher range at once, on your terms.
card_roles.Skyscribing: Prosperity with a forecast rider — a free-ish draw for everyone each upkeep from your hand, keeping hands topped up without spending the card.
card_roles.Braingeyser: Targeted X-draw: refill yourself, or force-feed one opponent over the Netsuke threshold at sorcery speed.
card_roles.Stroke of Genius: Braingeyser at instant speed — refill on an end step, or push a hand over 7 in response to their upkeep triggers going on the stack.
card_roles.Dig Through Time: Delve makes this two mana in the mid game: seven deep for exactly the two cards you need — usually a counter and a threat, or the buried Approach.
card_roles.Brass Infiniscope: A rock that pays you a card (and half-X life, doubled by the Archive) on your next X-spell — a small bridge between the ramp suite and the X-draw suite.
card_roles.Ghostly Prison: Pays for the deck's low creature count: attackers cost {2} each, and the whole table's mana is already stretched by your taxes.
card_roles.Propaganda: Ghostly Prison's blue twin. Two copies of this effect, The Second Doctor's no-attack rider, and punisher upkeep damage make attacking you the worst-value line at the table.
card_roles.Teferi's Protection: The panic button: life locked, everything phases out, you lose nothing to the wrath — and your engine board returns intact before your untap.
card_roles.Cyclonic Rift: The asymmetric reset. Overloaded on an end step it clears every opposing board while your punisher artifacts stay put.
card_roles.Swords to Plowshares: Premium one-mana creature exile; the life you give away comes back as upkeep damage.
card_roles.Path to Exile: The second one-mana exile. The basic land you gift is a real cost — save it for the creature that actually kills you.
card_roles.Loran of the Third Path: Artifact/enchantment removal on a body, plus a tap that draws you and an opponent a card — removal that also feeds the punishers, and the premium Displacer Kitten blink target for a re-triggered Disenchant.
card_roles.Torrential Gearhulk: Flash 5/6 that recasts a counterspell or Dig Through Time from the graveyard for free — a threat that interacts the turn it arrives.
card_roles.Leyline of Anticipation: Flash for everything before Heliod flips (and redundancy after) — free from the opening hand, which is when the deck most wants to play draw-go.
card_roles.Reliquary Tower: No maximum hand size on a land — redundant with The Second Doctor and Thought Vessel now, and the copy that survives every wrath.
card_roles.Mikokoro, Center of the Sea: A Temple Bell on a land: repeatable, uncounterable hand-stuffing that survives every board wipe.
card_roles.Homeward Path: Theft insurance on a land — everyone takes their own creatures back, which against the mind-control and theft decks usually means you take yours back.
card_roles.Lightning Greaves: Haste and shroud for Heliod or Hullbreaker Horror — protecting the flip turn is its main job here.

mulligan: The sim keeps 74.2% of first sevens and the deck mulligans gently (0.33 per game), so the bar is: two to four lands (the kept-hand distribution centers on 2–3 plus rocks — 18 lands means the nine rocks are load-bearing, and Ancient Tomb plus a two-drop rock is how 27.8% of games cast Heliod by turn 3), one card-flow piece, and something to say 'no' with. What you are actually mulliganing toward is flow plus interaction, not the combo: a table-draw engine is drawn by turn 6 in 72.3% of games (mean turn 2.6) and cheap or free interaction is held by then in 62.2% (73.3% of games ever) — those are the reliable axes, and Kwain now counts among the two-mana engines worth keeping a hand for. The full two-piece — engine PLUS punisher — is assembled by turn 6 in only 39.6% of games (better than the old build's 34.3%, still a minority), so never keep a marginal hand because it 'promises the lock'; the punishers are inert on their own (Iron Maiden reads hand minus 4 — against a normal hand that's one damage). Conversely, a hand of two punishers and no draw engine is a mulligan in costume. Ship it. Don't mulligan chasing Approach either — win-condition access is at 42.6% by turn 6 now that White Sun's Zenith is in the pool, and the correct response is trusting Mystical Tutor and Long-Term Plans to find it when the board is ready, not digging for it at hand-quality prices. Heliod himself needs no help — 90.8% of games cast him by turn 6, median turn 4 — so keep hands that use the turns before him: Remora into rock into Kami (or Kwain) is the curve the deck was built to play.
upgrades: The obsolescence index has real entries for this list's mana, and one clear target: Worn Powerstone. It's flagged as superseded by the two-mana Talisman class at lower cost — and the deck already owns the in-identity copies (Talisman of Progress, the Signets), so the actionable reading is that Powerstone is your first cut when trimming: it enters tapped, costs three, and stack 004's loop math also excludes it as an engine rock (the loop needs a castable two-drop that taps immediately). Azorius Signet's entry lists Mind Stone among its superseders — 'additional: draw' — a fair swap only if you value the late-game cash-in over colored fixing in a two-color deck; the index also flags Fellwar Stone as obsoleted by Sol Ring on cost, but you already run Sol Ring, and Fellwar's real demerit here is the verified one: it only sustains the Hullbreaker loop while an opponent's land can make mana. Long-Term Plans is indexed as obsoleted by Mystical Tutor, which you also already run — but the supersession is narrower than it looks, since Plans fetches any card (a punisher, Aetherflux) where Mystical only finds instants and sorceries; keep both. Counterspell draws entries for Syncopate and Spell Snare on cost alone — both are conditional counters by their own text, a poor trade in a deck that plans to hold mana anyway. Brass Infiniscope is flagged for Daily Bugle Newspaper (cheaper, with treasure and loot riders) — worth the swap if the X-spell rider rarely fires for you. The rebuild's four new cards were re-checked, and every one of their index entries fails the oracle-text test: Alhammarret's Archive is 'superseded' by Autograph Book, a pay-{3} counter-limited single draw with no doubling clause; Supreme Verdict by Devout Decree, a one-target color-hosed exile that is not a sweeper and not uncounterable; The Second Doctor by Sokka, Lateral Strategist, an attack-trigger draw body with no hand-size clause and no fort rider; Kwain by Erratic Visionary and Soothsayer Adept, plain looters with no table draw, no lifegain, and no politics. Similarity artifacts, all four — the clauses you added these cards for have no printed replacement. And the standing negative result holds: the punisher core itself — Iron Maiden, Ebony Owl Netsuke, Viseling, Howling Mine, Font of Mythos — has no obsolescence entries at all. Nothing printed since does this job better; the old cards are the tech, not the debt.
